opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've spent a lot of time on. The basic observation is that a lot of defenses that look robust aren't actually making the model robust. They're just making the gradient useless. When I run gradient descent to find an adversarial example and it fails, there are two very different explanations. One is that no adversarial example exists nearby, which is what the defense wants you to believe. The other is that adversarial examples exist everywhere, but my optimizer can't find them because the loss landscape has been made really ugly. Almost always it's the second one.

This shows up in a few ways. Sometimes the defense adds a non-differentiable step, like quantizing the input, JPEG-compressing it, or running some preprocessing whose gradient is zero almost everywhere. Sometimes it adds randomness, so every time you compute the gradient you get a different answer. Sometimes the model is so deep, or iterates some procedure so many times, that the gradients vanish or explode. In every case the defense isn't saying "this input is classified correctly." It's saying "good luck figuring out which direction to move."

The way I think about attacking these is that you shouldn't take the gradient the defense hands you at face value. You should ask what the defense is actually computing, and then find a better way to get a useful signal.

For the non-differentiable preprocessing, a really simple trick works surprisingly often. If the preprocessing step is roughly the identity, if JPEG compression gives you back something that looks basically like the input, then on the backward pass you just pretend it is the identity. You run the real thing forward and use the approximation backward. We called that BPDA, backward pass differentiable approximation. It feels like it shouldn't work, because you're using the wrong gradient, but it doesn't have to be exactly right. It just has to point roughly downhill.

For randomness, you average. If the defense randomly transforms the input, you compute the expected gradient over the randomness, and you optimize for an adversarial example that works in expectation. That's expectation over transformation. The defense isn't doing anything magical. It's just adding noise to your optimizer, and averaging removes noise.

For the very deep or iterative ones, you can often reparameterize the problem, or skip through the part that's causing trouble, or attack an earlier piece of the pipeline.

But the bigger lesson, the meta-lesson, is that you need to be adaptive. There's no universal attack that breaks every defense. You have to actually read the defense, understand the mechanism the authors think is making it robust, and then design the attack around that mechanism. A lot of papers evaluated against a fixed attack like standard PGD, saw it fail, and concluded they were robust. But the attack was never designed for that defense. If you take the time to understand it, most of these fall apart.

There are also some sanity checks I always tell people to run. If an unbounded attack doesn't hit 100% success, something is wrong with your attack, because with an unbounded perturbation you can just turn the image into a different class. If black-box or transfer attacks do better than white-box attacks, something is wrong, because you have strictly more information in the white-box setting. If increasing the perturbation budget doesn't steadily increase attack success, something is wrong. These are signs that you're looking at gradient masking, not robustness.

So my general stance is that a defense that makes gradients hard to optimize hasn't solved the problem. It has hidden it. And hidden problems tend to get found.

r001.rationale: The response says apparent robustness often comes from an ugly loss landscape or noisy gradients that prevent the optimizer from finding existing adversarial examples.

r002.rationale: It describes BPDA: use the actual preprocessing in the forward pass and an identity approximation in the backward pass to obtain a useful gradient for non-differentiable steps.

r003.rationale: The response does not connect resistance to fine-tuning with the rationale used for image adversarial examples in 2017.

r004.rationale: It discusses adapting attacks to difficult gradients, but does not mention models claimed to resist fine-tuning or overcoming their gradients through optimization adjustments.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've spent a lot of time on, and I think the short answer is that gradient masking is almost never a real defense, it's just a defense against one particular attack algorithm. When people build a defense that makes the gradients hard to optimize, what they've usually done is break the signal that gradient descent relies on, not actually make the model robust. The adversarial examples are still there. You just can't find them with the first thing you try.

So the way I think about it is: the attack has to be adapted to the defense. If someone adds a non-differentiable preprocessing step, like JPEG compression or bit-depth reduction, you can just approximate it with something differentiable on the backward pass, or in a lot of cases replace it with the identity function, and the attack goes right through. That's the whole BPDA idea. If the defense adds randomness, you don't attack one sample of the randomness, you take the expectation over it. If the gradients are numerically broken, vanishing or exploding because of some saturation trick, you can often fix that by changing the loss function or attacking the logits instead of the softmax output.

And then there's the tell-tale signs. If a defense claims robustness but a black-box attack does better than the white-box attack, that's not a robust model, that's a model where the gradients are lying to you. If increasing the perturbation budget to something enormous still doesn't get you to one hundred percent attack success, something is wrong. Those are the diagnostics I run before I even believe a claimed result.

The frustrating part is that this keeps happening. Every year there's another batch of papers that are, at some level, the same idea with a new coat of paint, and every year we go through and show that if you actually think about what the defense is doing, there's a straightforward attack. I don't think the people doing it are being dishonest. It's just that evaluating adversarial robustness is genuinely hard, and the default attack you pull off the shelf is not going to tell you whether your defense works. You have to actually try to break your own thing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses gradient masking, randomness, and numerically broken gradients, but does not identify a noisy, difficult-to-optimize loss surface as a common source of apparent robustness.

r002.rationale: It describes using a differentiable approximation on the backward pass for non-differentiable preprocessing to let the attack obtain usable gradients, which communicates the straight-through-estimator approach.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss resistance to fine-tuning or connect it to the defense rationale for image adversarial examples in 2017.

r004.rationale: It describes adapting attacks to difficult gradients, but does not address models claimed to resist fine-tuning or say that optimization adjustments overcome those gradients.

astra-6.text:
The first thing I ask is whether the defense actually makes the model more robust, or whether it just makes my particular attack harder to run. Those are very different things. If I try gradient descent and it fails, that tells me something about gradient descent on this system. It doesn’t necessarily tell me that there isn’t an adversarial example nearby.

So I try to understand what’s getting in the way. If the defense introduces randomness, I can average gradients over that randomness. If it has a step that’s nondifferentiable, I can sometimes use a differentiable approximation for the backward pass, while still evaluating the actual defense on the forward pass. The gradient doesn’t have to be perfectly accurate; it just has to point me in a useful direction.

And then I check whether the examples actually work against the full defended model. That’s the important part. You’re allowed to use approximations to find an attack, but success has to be measured on the real system.

More generally, I think you have to adapt the attack to the defense. Running an existing attack unchanged and watching it fail is a starting point for an evaluation, not the conclusion.

r001.rationale: The response discusses randomness and failed gradient descent, but does not identify a noisy, difficult-to-optimize loss surface as a common source of apparent robustness.

r002.rationale: It describes using a differentiable approximation in the backward pass for a nondifferentiable step to obtain a useful gradient, which communicates the estimator’s function.

r003.rationale: It does not connect resistance to fine-tuning with the defense rationale for image adversarial examples in 2017.

r004.rationale: It recommends adapting attacks to defenses, but does not state that optimization adjustments can overcome challenging gradients in models claimed to resist fine-tuning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to separate “this defense makes my attack fail” from “this defense actually makes the model robust.” Those are very different claims. If your attack relies on gradients, and the defense makes those gradients uninformative, you may have learned something about your optimizer rather than about the security of the model.

So I try to understand what’s causing the difficulty. Is there randomness? Is there a nondifferentiable operation? Is the loss just poorly behaved? Then I adapt the attack to that mechanism. You might average over the randomness, or use a smoother approximation to get a useful direction, while still checking whether the resulting example succeeds against the actual defense.

The important thing is that the defense doesn’t get to choose the attacker’s algorithm. If I can find another way to search that breaks it, then making the original gradient-based attack struggle wasn’t enough. And if I can’t break it, I want to be careful: that’s evidence about the attacks I tried, not automatically evidence that no attack exists.

r002.rationale: It suggests using a smoother approximation, but does not identify straight-through estimators as a way to obtain usable gradients.

r003.rationale: The response does not connect resistance to fine-tuning with the defense rationale for image adversarial examples in 2017.

r004.rationale: It says to adapt attacks and search by other means, but does not state that optimization adjustments can overcome challenging gradients in models claimed to resist fine-tuning.
